paragraphs: Some people do not think it is bad that heretics keep quiet about their opinions. They should first consider that, because of this silence, heretical opinions are never discussed fairly and completely. Some of these opinions could not survive such a discussion. But even if they are prevented from spreading, they do not disappear.

But the ban on any inquiry that does not reach the official conclusions does not harm heretics most. The greatest harm is done to people who are not heretics. Their whole mental development is limited, and their reason is frightened, by the fear of heresy. Who can calculate how much the world loses because many promising minds have timid characters? They do not dare to follow any bold, independent line of thought, in case it leads them to something irreligious or immoral. Among them we sometimes see a man with a deep conscience and a subtle, refined mind. He spends his life arguing with an intellect that he cannot silence. He uses all his cleverness to make his conscience and reason agree with official belief, perhaps without success.

Nobody can be a great thinker without recognising that his first duty as a thinker is to follow his mind to whatever conclusions it leads to. Truth gains more from the mistakes of someone who studies carefully and thinks for himself than from the true opinions of people who hold them only because they do not allow themselves to think.

But freedom of thought is not needed only, or mainly, to produce great thinkers. It is just as necessary, and even more so, to allow average people to reach the mental level they are capable of. There have been great individual thinkers in a general atmosphere of mental slavery, and there may be again. But in such an atmosphere there has never been, and never will be, an intellectually active people. When a people came close to this for a time, it was because the fear of unorthodox ideas was temporarily suspended. Sometimes people silently agree that principles must not be questioned, and that the greatest human questions are closed. Then we cannot expect the high level of mental activity that has made some periods of history so remarkable. When debate avoided subjects big enough to create enthusiasm, the mind of a people was never deeply stirred. It never received the push that raised even quite ordinary people to the dignity of thinking beings.

Europe offers three examples. The first is the period just after the Reformation. The second, limited to the Continent and to a more educated class, is the movement of ideas in the second half of the eighteenth century. The third, even shorter, is the intellectual excitement in Germany in the time of Goethe and Fichte. These periods developed very different opinions, but in all three the power of authority was broken. An old mental tyranny had been thrown off, and no new one had replaced it yet. The energy of these three periods has made Europe what it is today. Every improvement in the human mind or in institutions can be traced to one of them. For some time, however, all three impulses have seemed almost exhausted. We can expect no new start until we claim our mental freedom again.
